title: Airgap capacity + offline updates discussion - Lyra Therapeutics
customer_attendees: Aaron Kim - Head of ML Ops
summary: Discovery focused on Lyra's air-gapped on-prem needs: hardware constraints (power/cooling, NVMe sizing), offline update and patch process (signed manifests, USB/airgap bundles), compliance controls (audit logs, KMS/HSM integration), rollback/fallback, and runbook/monitoring expectations. Redwood AE/SE outlined Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs and required pre-install checklists. Customer requested an offline install checklist, appliance-like options, and a pilot agreement for two racks with a 3-month benchmark window.
topics: Hardware footprint & GPU choices (A100 vs H100)
Offline patching / signed bundles and update cadence
SLA and fallback to hosted during outages

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-05-09
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Tomas (Redwood SE), Linh (Redwood Sec), Aaron (Lyra), Priya (Lyra), Daniel (Lyra), Sofia (Lyra)
Links shared: security pack v2 (internal link), pilot-pricing-sheet.xlsx (link), airgap-manifest-example.tar.gz (link)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro - I'm Maya, AE at Redwood Inference. With me is Tomas, our SE, and Linh on security.
[00:12] Aaron: Hi, Aaron here. Head of ML Ops at Lyra. We're evaluating options for an on-prem air-gapped deployment for our model serving particularly because of IP/data residency needs.
[00:20] Priya: Priya, Security Architect. We'll be focused on the update processes and key management, also audit requirements.
[00:28] Tomas: Great, quick runframe: we'll ask about your constraints, walk through our airgap flow (bundles, manifests, signed updates), and then outline options — hosted vs dedicated vs private/appliance.
[00:40] Daniel: quick note — our infra is pretty constrained in two of our labs. limited power (power budget ~12kW per rack), single rack elevator access, and we prefer NVMe-only for the model DB. Also no standard internet egress.
[00:55] Linh: understood. we often see two patterns: a customer-run private deployment with a control plane inside customer's VPC (needs egress) or a fully airgapped private install where we provide signed install bundles and 운영 (korean?) — sorry, bad auto.
[01:14] Sofia: how do you patch kernels and runtime libs in airgapped? that's the blocker for us.
[01:20] Tomas: Two models. 1) Offline signed bundles: we generate a tarball with all containers, runtime libs and manifests, signed with our release key. You import via removable media. 2) Appliance-style: we ship an image that your infra team flashes to the nodes. Both require a verification step against public key material we provisioned earlier.
[01:38] Aaron: So there's a public key that we keep, and you provide signed artifacts — sounds good. How do we handle emergency hotfixes if something critical breaks?
[01:47] Tomas: We have a process for airgap hotfixes: small delta packages with clear manifests and a signed hash. The recommended cadence is weekly from our side for security patches during pilot, but we can do ad-hoc urgent bundles. Each bundle has a signed manifest and a rollback label.
[02:05] Priya: And for regulatory audit we need immutable logs of who applied what and when, and preferably the ability to ship logs to our central SIEM that sits outside the airgapped zone — but that would be a one-way export, is that supported?
[02:22] Linh: We support export of audit logs via a controlled export tool that writes to a removable drive with sequence numbers and signatures. We also can stream to syslog if temporary controlled egress is allowed, but we understand many customers only want removable media exports.
[02:40] Daniel: On hardware — we are debating A100 vs H100. H100 is newer but our scheduling and power envelope might favor A100. Thoughts?
[02:49] Tomas: H100 brings perf wins for certain FP16 ops, but for inference at low latency A100 is still solid and may be more cost-effective on power. Also for quantized int8 workloads, kernel support matters; we’ll map model ops to runtime kernels during onboarding. We should run a quick benchmark with your models to see real-world numbers.
[03:12] Aaron: what's the NVMe sizing you'd recommend for KV cache and model shards?
[03:18] Tomas: Recommendation starts at 4TB NVMe per GPU for large models if you plan to shard and keep KV caches persistently, but many customers run with 2TB/GPU and rely on hot reloading. Given your research workload, I'd recommend 6TB/GPU for comfort. We'll validate with an initial profiling run.
[03:38] Priya: KMS integration — we use an on-prem HSM and cannot expose keys. can Redwood integrate with a local HSM or key escrow?
[03:46] Linh: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS/HSM. For airgap installs we provide a local KMS connector that talks to your HSM via the allowed network segment. We also support encrypted key material that is loaded at install time and never egressed. The private deploy has hooks for PKCS#11 and KMIP.
[04:05] Sofia: How about automatic fallback — say a node goes bad and models need to be served from hosted for a short time, is that possible when airgapped?
[04:13] Tomas: If you want fallback to our hosted cluster, that requires controlled egress and contract language — we can design a hybrid where critical queries can route out via a proxy. But true airgap by definition disallows that; instead we prefer redundancy in-rack and cross-rack failover. You could also set up an intermediate staging network that allows limited egress for failover under tightly controlled conditions.
[04:40] Aaron: Ok. Procurement will ask about patch verification, chain of custody for install media. how do you sign/verify?
[04:47] Linh: All bundles have SHA256 signatures and are signed with our private release key. We provide the public key fingerprint ahead of time. For chain of custody we recommend checksums printed on manifests and an internal acceptance checklist that your ops team signs off against. We'll share a template.
[05:06] Daniel: Observability — what telemetry runs in the airgapped instance? CPU/GPU metrics, token-level latency traces, per-route QPS?
[05:14] Tomas: We ship a local collector that stores metrics in a time-series DB on-prem. Dashboards run locally in the console. For audits you export snapshots. We can also compress and sign metric exports for ingestion into your central analytics in batches via removable media.
[05:34] Priya: Data retention — logs and prompts; how long are those kept? We need options to TTL data at 30 days and ensure redaction for PII.
[05:43] Linh: Retention is configurable at route-level; you can set TTLs, enable redaction hooks, and disable prompt storage entirely if needed. Everything is configurable before install in the manifest.
[05:56] Aaron: Service/support — if we go with a pilot, what does 24/7 look like for an airgapped private deployment?
[06:02] Maya: Pilot support package includes extended windows with guaranteed response SLAs for P1/P2. On-call rotations are covered and we offer optional dedicated SE hours for the pilot. For airgap installs we often provide an on-site engineer for first-week ramp.
[06:18] Daniel: Any regulatory certifications we should be aware of? SOC2 is relevant for us.
[06:23] Linh: Redwood has SOC2 Type II and ISO in progress; for airgap/private we add a specific controls appendix. We'll provide the compliance pack.
[06:33] Aaron: timeline — we aim to have a pilot in Q3, procurement by end of May. Can you meet that?
[06:40] Maya: Yes, if we finalize scope this week we can slot engineering ramp and schedule the pilot for mid-July. We'll need the rack spec and PO to lock dates.
[06:51] Sofia: Downtime for updates — what's the recommended maintenance window?
[06:56] Tomas: We design bundles to be largely rolling-update friendly. For major runtime changes a short maintenance window (15-45 minutes) per shard may be needed, but many patches can be applied with zero downtime depending on your redundancy. We'll provide runbooks for both rolling and cold updates.
[07:17] Aaron: Are there any limitations on models — footprints, custom kernels, or open-source licensing we should worry about?
[07:24] Tomas: We support standard architectures and many popular OSS checkpoints. Custom kernels are supported via an integration process during onboarding; we validate and sign kernels before they run. Licensing: we require confirmation you have rights to the models, and we'll provide guidance on third-party license compliance.
[07:40] Priya: Ok last security deep dive question: if an operator has compromised machine access, can they exfiltrate keys or model weights from the appliance?
[07:51] Linh: Keys never leave the HSM in plaintext. Model weights are stored encrypted at rest; decryption keys are scoped to process memory and cleared on restart. That lowers the risk of persistent exfil — but we still recommend host hardening and full-disk encryption on NVMe.
[08:10] Daniel: for the pilot, we need an initial BOM: node types, GPU qty, NVMe per node, network top-of-rack, and power draw. can you produce a recommended BOM?
[08:19] Tomas: We'll produce a recommended BOM based on your workload profile — we'll start with 2 racks, 6x A100 80GB per rack as a baseline and adjust after profiling. We'll include power/thermal and physical install notes.
[08:33] Maya: quick commercial note — pilot pricing will include the private deploy license, pilot support, and optional on-site engineer days. We'll get that out in a separate sheet.
[08:44] Aaron: Great. Are there any blockers you see right away?
[08:48] Tomas: only dependency is that we need the rack power numbers and whether you allow removable media imports at the facility. The latter is a hard constraint for airgap.
[09:00] Priya: We can allow removable media but it needs to go through chain-of-custody and scanning. That works.
[09:06] Sofia: one more — latency expectations for retrieval-heavy research workloads?
[09:11] Tomas: We'll profile, but expect single-digit to low-double-digit ms for local NVMe-attached caches; cross-shard fetches add more. We'll tune caching and KV lifetimes to match your workload.
[09:27] Maya: ok, recap of next steps: Tomas shares install checklist + BOM draft, Maya shares pilot pricing and SOW, Priya to confirm procurement timeline and confirm removable media policy.
[09:39] Aaron: sounds good. Thanks.
[09:42] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and propose times for the install workshop.

End of transcript

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words ("oper-ate" for "operate"), system replaced some product names with similar sounding words. There was minor crosstalk around hardware specifics.
